Extract a Ui class for talking to the user
commitResults.messageBody:
First step of A-MoreOOP. Elsa had grown to 444 lines and was doing everything:
reading the keyboard, wording every message, drawing the borders, parsing
commands and carrying them out. This moves the first of those concerns out.

Ui is now the only class that touches System.out or the keyboard. It owns the
border, the indentation, the banner, the greeting, the farewell and the error
prefix, and it exposes one method per thing the chatbot can say: showWelcome,
showAdded, showRemoved, showMarked, showUnmarked, showTasks, showTasksOn,
showSkippedLines and showError. Elsa now says what happened and lets Ui decide
how it is worded and laid out, so a change to the wording or the layout is made
in one file.

Reading input moved as well, since typing is as much an interaction with the
user as printing is. Ui owns the Scanner and offers hasNextCommand and
readCommand, which reads Elsa's loop better than the Scanner calls did.

Ui was made an instance class rather than a bag of static methods, both because
it holds the Scanner and because the target design in the exercise constructs
it. Elsa keeps it in a local variable for now; turning Elsa itself into an
object with ui, storage and tasks as fields is a later step, so that this one
change can be checked on its own.

The formatting of the two task listings moved into Ui as showTasks and
showTasksOn rather than staying behind as string builders, so that the
boundary is a clean one: no message text is left in Elsa at all. The cost is
that Ui knows about ArrayList<Task>, which will become a TaskList when that
class is extracted.

Elsa is 298 lines from 444, and all 24 UI test cases still pass, which is the
point of a refactoring: the behaviour is untouched and the tests needed no
edits.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a Parser class for reading typed commands
commitResults.messageBody:
Second step of A-MoreOOP. After Ui was pulled out, what remained in Elsa was
still two jobs mixed together: working out what a typed line means, and doing
something about it. This separates them.

Parser now owns everything that turns text into values. It splits a line into a
Command and its arguments, reads the arguments of todo, deadline and event
straight into the matching Task, reads a task number into a list index, and
reads a date. The /by, /from and /to separators moved with it, as did the six
checking helpers that word the errors when a part is missing, empty, not a
number, not a date, or holds the text that separates fields in the data file.

The parse methods return finished objects rather than pieces for the caller to
assemble: parseDeadline hands back a Deadline, not a description and a date. So
Elsa no longer knows that a deadline is written with /by, and a change to how a
command is typed does not touch Elsa at all. Three branches of the switch are
now one line each.

parseLine returns a ParsedLine record holding the command and its arguments,
rather than two methods each splitting the line again. This follows the record
already used for Storage.LoadResult.

Parser deliberately does not touch the task list or the disk, and it throws
ElsaException with wording meant for the user, so Elsa can hand any failure to
Ui without knowing what went wrong.

Elsa is 111 lines from 298, and reads as what it now is: load the list, read a
line, dispatch it, report anything that failed. The NOTHING and UNKNOWN cases
stay in the switch, since those are about dispatch rather than about reading
arguments.

All 24 UI test cases still pass unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract a TaskList class holding the tasks
commitResults.messageBody:
Third step of A-MoreOOP. The tasks were kept in a plain ArrayList that Elsa,
Storage and Ui all reached into directly, each doing its own get, size and
remove. Any code holding that list could have cleared or reordered it, and
nothing said where the rules about it belonged.

TaskList now owns the list and keeps it private. It offers size, isEmpty, get,
add, delete, mark and unmark, and nothing hands the underlying ArrayList out,
so the list can only be changed through those methods. delete, mark and unmark
return the task they acted on, which is what the caller needs in order to show
the user what happened; Elsa no longer fetches the task a second time after
changing it, as the mark and unmark branches did.

Two constructors match the two ways a session can start: an empty list on a
first run or after a failed load, and a list built from tasks already read from
the disk. Storage.load now returns a TaskList inside its LoadResult and
Storage.save takes one, so the loaded tasks arrive in the form the rest of the
program uses them in rather than being converted at each call site. Ui shows a
TaskList for the same reason.

TaskList deliberately does not save itself after a change. Making add and
delete write to the disk would remove the repeated Storage.save calls in Elsa,
but a collection that quietly performs file writes is a surprising thing to
hand to someone, and it would tie the list to there being a disk at all. The
repetition is better removed by giving Elsa the storage as a field, which is
the next step.

Elsa is 107 lines and no longer imports ArrayList at all: it holds no
collections, only the objects that own them.

All 24 UI test cases still pass unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Make Elsa an object rather than one static main
commitResults.messageBody:
Fourth step of A-MoreOOP. Elsa was a class only in name: a single static main
holding the whole session, with ui and tasks as local variables that had to be
passed into every helper. addTask(ui, tasks, task) took two parameters that
were the same on every call, which is what a field is for.

Elsa now has ui and tasks as fields, and main is one line: new Elsa().run().
addTask(task) takes only what varies. run() reads as the shape of a session:
greet, load, then read and carry out commands until told to stop.

The 60 line switch moved out of the loop into execute(), which returns whether
to carry on. This keeps each method to one job: run() decides how long the
session lasts, execute() decides what one command does. It also removes the
isRunning flag being assigned from inside the switch, since the BYE branch now
returns false where before it reached out and changed a variable in the
enclosing loop.

The design differs from the one in the exercise in one way. There, the
constructor loads the tasks and reports a loading error. Here, the constructor
only makes an empty chatbot and run() loads. Two reasons: the greeting must
appear before any complaint about the saved file, which cannot happen if
loading is done during construction; and making an object should not by itself
read from the disk, since that gives the constructor a way to fail at something
unrelated to constructing. loadTasks() is a private method called at the start
of run(), so the ordering is stated where it matters.

Storage is left as a static class for now. Making it an instance with an
injected file path is worth doing, but Parser and Ui both call
Storage.getFileName() statically to name the file in their messages, so that
change needs a decision about those two call sites and belongs in its own step.

All 24 UI test cases still pass unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Make Storage an object told which file to use
commitResults.messageBody:
Fifth and last step of A-MoreOOP. Storage was a static class with the file name
built into it, so there was exactly one place the tasks could ever live and no
way to point it anywhere else, including from a test.

Storage now has a constructor taking the path, and save, load and getFileName
are instance methods. Elsa holds one as a field and passes "data/elsa.txt" from
a constant beside main, so the one decision about where the tasks live is made
at the program's starting point rather than buried in the class that happens to
do the writing. Elsa's own constructor takes the path too, matching the shape
the exercise gives, so a caller could run a chatbot over a different file.

The path is kept twice inside Storage, as the text the caller wrote and as a
Path built from it. That is deliberate: Path.toString() renders with the
separator of whichever operating system is running, so a message built from it
would read data\elsa.txt on Windows and data/elsa.txt elsewhere, and the
recorded test output could only match on one of them. Keeping the original text
for messages avoids that. Forward slashes are accepted by every platform, so
Path.of on the given string is safe.

Two callers reached Storage.getFileName() statically and had to be dealt with.

Ui is now told the file name as a parameter to showSkippedLines. That warning
tells the user which file to go and edit, so naming it earns its place, and
Elsa has both objects to hand.

Parser no longer names the file at all. Its message now says the text cannot be
used "because that is how the parts of a stored task are separated" rather than
naming data/elsa.txt. Passing a file name through parseTodo, parseDeadline and
parseEvent would have put storage details into three signatures that have
nothing to do with storage, and the rule being explained is about the format,
not about the file. A parser has no business knowing that a file exists.

This changes four lines of expected output in TC-19, which is a deliberate
change to the wording rather than a regression, so the test plan was updated to
match. All 24 cases pass.

The minimal A-MoreOOP target is now met: Ui, Storage, Parser and TaskList each
own one concern, and Elsa is left holding the order they happen in.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename Storage.parseTask to readSavedTask
commitResults.messageBody:
The name invited the reader to think this method was Parser's job leaking into
Storage. It is not: Parser reads the language the user types, loosely written
and reported back with usage hints, while this method reads the file format
that the save methods in the same class write, reported back by line number and
field count. The two change for different reasons, which is why they live
apart, but sharing the word "parse" hid that.

readSavedTask names the language it reads, and pairs with Task.toSaveFormat(),
which it is the reverse of. A note on the method says so, so the next reader
does not have to ask.

The method is private and no output changed. All 24 UI test cases pass.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename the Command enum to CommandType
commitResults.messageBody:
Preparing for the A-MoreOOP stretch goal, which asks for an abstract Command
class with a subclass per command. The name Command is currently taken by the
enum, and the two mean different things: the enum is the vocabulary of the
language, saying which words are commands and how each is written, while the
class the stretch goal wants is the behaviour, saying what one does.

CommandType says what the enum is for, and frees the name for the class that
carries the behaviour. Nothing else changes: the enum keeps its keyword and
usage pairs, which the parser still needs in order to word its errors, and
which have nothing to do with executing anything.

Renaming on its own, before any of the new classes exist, keeps the change
mechanical and reviewable. All 24 UI test cases pass unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give each command its own class
commitResults.messageBody:
The A-MoreOOP stretch goal. Every command's behaviour lived in one switch in
Elsa, so nine unrelated things sat in one method and adding a command meant
editing it. Each command is now a class that knows how to carry itself out.

Command is abstract, with execute(tasks, ui, storage) and isExit(). The three
things a command might need are handed to execute rather than held as fields,
because a command is built by the parser, which has none of them, and run later
by the chatbot, which has all three. isExit() answers false by default, so only
ExitCommand has to say otherwise and a new command ends the session only if it
means to.

Parser.parse now returns one of these. Its switch chooses which class to build
and no longer says what any of them does, so it gains a line when a command is
added and changes for no other reason. parseTodo, parseDeadline, parseEvent,
parseDate and parseLine became private: parse is the only way in.

Elsa.run is now the loop the exercise describes: read a line, parse it, execute
it, ask whether to stop. Elsa's execute() and addTask() are gone, and Elsa is
95 lines holding only the shape of a session.

One check had to move. parseTaskIndex used to check both that a task number was
a whole number and that a task with it existed, but the second needs the list,
which the parser does not have. Parser.parseTaskNumber now checks the writing
and returns the number as typed, and TaskNumberCommand, the shared parent of
mark, unmark and delete, checks that the number means something when the
command runs and the list is in front of it. The order the user sees is
unchanged, since parsing still happens before executing.

AddCommand covers todos, deadlines and events, because adding is the same work
whichever kind of task it is; what differs is how they are written, which is
the parser's concern.

The loop keeps this project's message blocks rather than the showLine() calls in
the exercise's example. Ui already draws a border on both sides of every block,
so calling showLine() around each command would print empty bordered blocks for
commands that say nothing.

Nine new classes, and all 24 UI test cases pass unchanged.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract TaskFormat, so one class owns the saved line format
commitResults.messageBody:
Storage was doing two jobs: handling the file, and knowing what a line in it
means. Those change for different reasons, and adding a field to the format had
no business touching the code that creates directories.

Worse, nothing owned the format at all. Task, Todo, Deadline and Event each
wrote a line with the separator, the done markers and the type letter spelled
out again as literals, and Storage read all of them with its own copies of the
same literals. Six files repeated the same strings, so the writing and the
reading could drift apart and nothing would catch it until a saved task failed
to load.

TaskFormat now names the separator, the two done markers and the three type
letters once. The task classes write with those names instead of literals, and
TaskFormat.decode reads with the same ones, so a change to any of them reaches
both directions. The field counts are named too, rather than 3, 4 and 5
appearing bare in the checks. Splitting a line now uses Pattern.quote on the
separator instead of a hand written " \| " regex, which removes the second place
the separator was spelled out and the escaping that went with it.

Storage is 151 lines from 241 and is about the file: whether it exists, making
its folder, reading its lines, writing them back, and turning an IOException
into something the user can read.

The two directions stay asymmetrical, and the class comment says so. Writing is
polymorphic, since each task knows how it is written. Reading has to see a type
letter before it knows what to build, so it is one switch. Adding a task type
means editing TaskFormat as well as writing the new class, which a factory or a
registry could avoid at a cost in machinery that three task types do not
justify.

Parser now checks user input against TaskFormat.SEPARATOR rather than
Storage.SEPARATOR, which is also a better dependency: it was never the file it
cared about, only the format.

All 24 UI test cases pass, and a save and reload round trip was checked by hand.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch-A-MoreOOP into master
Organise the classes into packages
commitResults.messageBody:
Twenty two classes sat in the default package, which says nothing about how
they relate and is not something a real project would do. They are now under
one elsa package, split by the roles the earlier refactoring separated:

  elsa            Elsa, ElsaException, Dates
  elsa.command    Command, CommandType and the eight command classes
  elsa.task       Task, Todo, Deadline, Event, TaskList, TaskFormat
  elsa.parser     Parser
  elsa.storage    Storage
  elsa.ui         Ui

src/main/java stays the source root, so the packages are directories under it.

TaskFormat went into elsa.task rather than the elsa.storage it might seem to
belong to. The four task classes write their lines with its constants and
Storage reads lines through it, so putting it with Storage would have made
task and storage depend on each other in both directions. In elsa.task the
arrow runs one way, storage to task, and TaskFormat sits beside the
toSaveFormat methods that are its other half.

Dates and ElsaException stayed in the root package because every other package
uses them, so putting them in any one package would have made that package a
dependency of all the rest.

Three javadoc links were reworded to plain prose: TaskFormat naming Storage,
and Command and AddCommand naming Parser. A {@link} needs an import to resolve,
so those three links alone had task depending on storage and command depending
on parser, in the direction that should not exist. The classes are still named
in the text, just not linked. No sibling packages now depend on each other in
both directions; only the conventional parent and child dependency between
elsa and its sub-packages remains.

No access modifier was widened to make this compile, so nothing was opened up
that was not already public.

The test plan's run command is now java src/main/java/elsa/Elsa.java, which the
Java 25 source launcher resolves against the source root and follows into the
sub-packages. The saved file is still data/elsa.txt, since a relative path is
resolved against the folder the program runs in and has nothing to do with
packages, so no expected output changed. All 24 UI test cases pass.
